headline: BHP outperforming Rio on the day due to ~50% earnings exposure to elevated copper prices
reasoning: Ryan Lim highlights that BHP has roughly 50% of earnings tied to copper, which is currently buoyed by elevated copper prices, giving it a larger copper earnings uplift than Rio Tinto. This explains BHP's stronger daily performance (+3% vs Rio's +1.5%) following Rio's production update. BHP is described as still undergoing a transformation, having pursued copper more aggressively than Rio.
quote: BHP has like roughly about 50% of the earnings tied into copper. Again, this is sort of like buoyed by the elevated copper prices. So production lines, I think, iron ore is still very much a large division from an asset perspective. But from Rio Tinto you've got copper only representing like 15, 20, I think 25% of the business. So a much smaller component.

headline: Ryan Lim flags CBA's August results as a potential negative surprise on provisioning costs relative to consensus expectations
reasoning: Ryan Lim singles out CBA's upcoming August results as a likely negative catalyst, with consensus currently underestimating the step-up in provision costs. He also notes the Juno update confirmed asset quality concerns are real. By November he expects the market to fully understand the deteriorating asset quality trajectory, which is inconsistent with the current index valuation.
quote: Coming into August, I think CBA's results is going to be potentially a surprise or consensus numbers based on where they are projecting provision costs at the moment. Very much by November period, I think the market will have more or less have a good understanding of actually where the asset quality story is going, which is not in the right direction of where the index is currently trading at the moment.

headline: Evolution Mining's cost of production broadly in line with expectations at ~A$1,700/oz but faces headwinds from elevated energy costs and softening gold prices
reasoning: Ryan Lim noted that Evolution Mining's cost curve came in broadly in line with Alpha Insights' estimates at around A$1,700/oz cost of production. However, he flagged that energy costs are weighing on the miner and that gold prices have softened from near A$4,500-5,000 levels, with investor appetite for gold also easing. These factors represent a headwind for Evolution going forward.
quote: Well, this is where we start to see more of the impact of the energy costs. Impacts are weighing on the miner. Against our own estimates anyway, the cost curve for even has come in broadly in line with expectations at around 1700 cost of production. I think also you've got the backdrop of softening gold prices. We have been sort of like sounding out that, you know, gold prices could stay elevated at above the five, like near the four and a half, 5000 levels. And we've seen that sort of come back down and in line with that I guess sentiment or investor appetite for gold has sort of softer, not abated a little bit as well.

headline: Rio Tinto copper cost guidance halved due to elevated gold byproduct credits, but copper remains a smaller share of the business than BHP
reasoning: Ryan Lim notes the key takeaway from Rio's production update is that copper cost guidance has essentially halved over the period, driven by gold byproduct credits stemming from elevated gold prices. Copper only represents around 15-25% of Rio's earnings, making it a much smaller driver than at BHP. He also flagged elevated diesel and haulage costs coming through in Rio's operational update, which investors need to factor into cost estimates ahead of the August reporting season. Additionally, Rio flagged strong lithium demand, with battery energy storage now overtaking EVs as the primary demand driver for lithium.
quote: So Rio's update is really a BHP update in my opinion, because one of the key takeaways in Rio's update is actually with regards to their copper cross guidance, which has essentially halved um, over the period due to byproducts, stemming from the elevated gold prices, helping to sort of keep costs subdued on the copper division. And that has actually translated to BHP doing better than Rio today, being up 3%, while Rio Tinto is only up 1.5%.

headline: Ryan Lim warns Australian major banks are overvalued with rising provisioning costs set to surprise consensus in upcoming results seasons
reasoning: Ryan Lim believes Australian major banks are overvalued and has been flagging asset quality concerns for some time. Provision costs have been subdued since Covid but are now beginning to rise, with banks only starting to recognise higher provisioning in the May reporting season. The Juno update further confirmed asset quality concerns are real. He expects CBA's August results to potentially disappoint consensus on provision costs, and by November the broader market will have a clearer picture of the worsening asset quality trajectory.
quote: Definitely regard the major banks as overvalued. We've been harping on about the asset quality issues in the major banks. We talked about the provision costs being very subdued across the major banks for quite some time now, ever since the Covid pandemic. Only in the May reporting season are we starting to see banks recognize that, higher provisioning costs. And then obviously going into June, you have the Juno update as well, which classify the asset quality concerns are very much real. Provision costs are probably going to step up. So coming into August, I think CBA's results is going to be potentially a surprise or consensus numbers based on where they are projecting provision costs at the moment. Very much by November period, I think the market will have more or less have a good understanding of actually where the asset quality story is going, which is not in the right direction of where the index is currently trading at the moment.

headline: Alpha Insights' AI-driven fundamental valuation finds the ASX 200 index trading ~30% above intrinsic value
reasoning: Ryan Lim described an exercise in which Alpha Insights used AI to value each of the 200 companies making up the ASX 200 index. The aggregate result showed the index trading approximately 30% above the composite intrinsic or book value estimate. He noted the index weighting is heavily skewed toward mining and banks. He acknowledged that global markets are heavily influenced by US AI/tech themes (Mag 7, GPUs, data centres), making it difficult to distinguish real value, but concluded the result reaffirms his long-held view that there is significant 'hot air' in the index.
quote: We've actually managed to value each and every one of the two other companies that make up the ASX 200. At the time of our analysis, the ASX 200 was the index itself anyway was about 30% above, say, the book value or the intrinsic valuation of the index, according to Alpha Insights. Now most people might say, well, that's your valuation. But I think in the grand scheme of things, we're playing this across, you know, 200 different companies. And obviously the weighting is very much around the mining and the banks as well. But based on the scale, I think there's some it helps to sort of reaffirm that idea that, you know, there may be some hot air in the index that needs to be laid out.

headline: Battery energy storage is overtaking EVs as the primary demand driver for lithium, per Rio Tinto's update
reasoning: Ryan Lim highlighted that Rio Tinto's production update explicitly noted strong lithium demand, but the driver has shifted away from EV sales toward battery energy storage systems. He views this as a meaningful structural observation for the lithium sector going forward.
quote: The last one, which is I think the most interesting takeaway is just around the lithium division. Rio Tinto has come out saying that lithium demand has remained quite strong. The drivers of lithium demand this time around hasn't been so much around EV sales, but around energy storage or battery storage or battery as an energy storage asset. The battery demand is definitely overtaking the EV as the driver going forward for lithium. And you know, we've seen that reflected in the Rio Tinto update.

headline: Ryan Lim sees global equity markets as approximately 30% overvalued, driven by AI and data centre themes inflating index weights
reasoning: Ryan Lim undertook a fundamental valuation exercise and found the broader index is around 30% overvalued. He attributes much of this to the AI, semiconductor, and data centre themes that are driving global markets, largely via US mega-cap stocks. He views the index as containing significant 'hot air' that makes it difficult to distinguish real value from inflated valuations.
quote: Coming in at 30% over valuation for the index is a bit surprising. I mean, not necessarily as well, but it sort of just helps to reaffirm the perspective that I've held for quite some time, which is that, you know, we're in a overvalued territory. Those are governed by what's happening in the US, being led by, you know, the AI, the medic, and the GPUs and data center themes. So with all these mixed into, I guess, this massive melting pot, like sometimes it's very hard to distinguish what is real value, what is not real value.

headline: Elevated diesel and haulage costs are a system-wide issue for Australian miners heading into August reporting season
reasoning: Ryan Lim flagged that diesel costs have been elevated across the mining system, noting this is evident in both Rio Tinto's and Evolution Mining's operational updates. He cautioned that consensus cost estimates may be too low and investors need to revise upward their cost assumptions ahead of the August reporting season.
quote: The other key takeaway that, well, there's are two more key takeaways from Rio's update. Firstly, it's around diesel costs. So these would cost has been quite elevated across the system. And that has now reflected the Rio Tinto's I guess operational updates. And to an extent as well, this would also have been evidence in Evans update as well. So cost and haulage, um, prices are uh, much elevated there. So I guess consensus or investors have to be more mindful around where their cost estimates are placed going into the August reporting season.
